> oh, but also, when we subset the dataset we subset both the index and the coordinate.

Hmm normally slicing a dataset or dataarray should first slice the index (via the index's `.isel()`) then create the new index coordinate(s) via the new index's `.create_variables()`. Like most operations that involve the creation of a new, derived index.

> How do you propose we proceed here?

Let's keep relying on the internals here, that's fine. Although I wouldn't recommend that elsewhere :-).

oh, but also, when we subset the dataset we subset both the index and the coordinate. The index returns a copy of itself (which is cheap in terms of memory), but that means that the coordinate does the same thing again.

Do you know if we can somehow replace the coordinate with a new coordinate to avoid the second slice? Or is that only a problem if we pulled out the coordinate into a `DataArray`?
agreed, I don't feel too comfortable reaching into xarray's internals either (even though we're in the privileged situation of having a hand in both libraries). How do you propose we proceed here?

> Finally I didn't know whether the forward / backward framing of CoordinateTransform made sense for this kind of array: we basically just want to sync any indexing operations with the index.

Agreed that doesn't make a lot of sense. A generic array indexing adapter that wraps an Xarray index would make better sense, and I'm wondering if/how we could publicly expose such functionality in Xarray... Best way would be to refactor and make public the whole explicit indexing logic (which if I remember correctly was part of the NamedArray topix on the roadmap? Or as a follow-up?), but that's a pretty big task. In the meantime, maybe we could provide something similar to CoordinateTransform? I.e., a public "intermediate" class that is wrapped in an internal indexing adapter... Not sure exactly how it would look, though.

the reason is that `_oindex_get` and `_vindex_get` explicitly convert to `numpy.ndarray`, which I'd like to avoid here (see the `np.asarray` at the end of both function implementations).

`_vindex_get` will probably never be able to get called here because vectorized indexing is, as far as I understand it, inherently n-dimensional (I also don't think we need to care about the case of indexing with a multidimensional array for now).

Finally I didn't know whether the forward / backward framing of `CoordinateTransform` made sense for this kind of array: we basically just want to sync any indexing operations with the index. After that it is the index that produces the values, and we don't really go from label space to index space. So at that point the existing class felt a bit too rigid / unsuitable (but I may definitely be missing something).

Nice!

I haven't looked at the implementation in detail yet, just a couple of questions below on the need of implementing a separate indexing adapter vs. reusing Xarray's CoordinateTransform / CoordinateTransformIndex. This shouldn't be a blocker, though!

> slicing the coordinate will not compute

This is indeed desirable. It can be supported using CoordinateTransform based indexes as well, so far only partially though. For example `xarray.indexes.RangeIndex` has a `.slice()` method added to the coordinate transform class, called via the index's `.isel()` method. This doesn't work when directly slicing the array indexing adapter or the Xarray variable, but it should work for the common cases like slicing the DataArray, which internally call the index's `.isel()`.

Anyway it would be good idea to have better slicing support in the Xarray coordinate transform base classes:

- add a `CoordinateTransform.slice()` method with an optional implementation (by default raise `NotImplementedError`)
- add a default implementation of `CoordinateTransformIndex.isel()` check and call `.slice()` of the wrapped coordinate transform object
- also in `CoordinateTransformIndexingAdapter._oindex_get()` check and call `.slice()` of the wrapped coordinate transform object

> the coordinate is strictly 1D, thus _vindex_get is not supported (for now, at least)

In that case CoordinateTransformIndexingAdapter returns a numpy array and CoordinateTransformIndex drops the index, which is also the behavior with a strict 1-dimensional coordinate associated with a default (pandas) index. I was wondering if there is a specific reason to instead explicitly raise here?

> transpose is either a no-op or raises because multiple values were passed

Isn't there already an error raised upper in the stack when multiple values were passed, e.g., via `Variable.transpose()`? 
In the 1-dimensional case it is almost a no-op as well in CoordinateTransformIndexingAdapter (just a shallow copy by passing through the wrapped CoordinateTransform object).


Apart from that, are there other reasons for the moc index to have its own indexing adapter instead of using Xarray's CoordinateTransform that I'm missing?

actually, there might be an argument for the conventions to work on the objects themselves (`encode` already does that): `cf` may add `grid_mapping` to all variables that have the spatial dimension, which we'd have to remove that after decoding because that variable does not exist anymore. So that would mean we'd get a signature of:
```python
class Convention:
    def decode(
        self,
        ds: xr.Dataset,
        *,
        grid_info: dict | DGGSInfo | None = None,
        name: Hashable | None = None,
        index_options: dict | None = None
    ) -> xr.Dataset:
        """
        Decode the dataset according to the convention.

        Parameters
        ----------
        ds : xr.Dataset
            The encoded dataset.
        grid_info : mapping or DGGSInfo, optional
             Overrides for the grid metadata.
        name : str, optional
            The name of the cell ids coordinate.
        index_options : mapping of str to Any, optional
            Additional options for the index.

        Returns
        -------
        decoded : xr.Dataset
            The decoded dataset with a DGGSIndex.
        """
        pass

    def encode(self, ds: xr.Dataset, *, encoding: dict | None = None) -> xr.Dataset:
        """
        Encode according to the convention.

        Parameters
        ----------
        ds : xr.Dataset
            The dataset to encode. Must have a DGGSIndex.
        encoding : mapping of str to Any, optional
            Additional options for the convention.

        Returns
        -------
        encoded : xr.Dataset
            The encoded dataset. Does not have a DGGSIndex anymore.
        """
        pass
```
(the convention shouldn't have to deal with the differences between `DataArray` and `Dataset`)

In theory, the `grid_info` and `name` kwargs could be packed into a `encoding` kwarg to make the method signatures symmetrical.

@benbovy, I've implemented the changes we discussed yesterday (I'll add documentation / type hints to the `Convention` base class later).

However, now that we normalize to the "xdggs" convention, we can probably change `Convention.decode` to return a `grid_info` object and the `cell_ids` variable, and have `decode` (the accessor method / top-level function) create the index. The only problem with that is that then it is `xdggs` that needs to know how to create the underlying index for compressed coordinates.

Otherwise we could have backends call `DGGSIndex.from_variables` directly.

So this clearly needs some more thought to create a clean API, especially if we want people to create their own convention implementations.
(also, if you notice anything that's wrong / broken, I don't mind iterating quickly)

"grid" in this case refers to an array of plots (or facet plot, for the definition of that see e.g. matplotlib), and thus to a widget design layout element and not a geospatial grid. Basically, what I'm trying to do is arrange multiple maps in some kind of table to be able to compare data visually.

"map" and "layer" follow the definitions of lonboard, where "layer" is a set of geometries / data and "map" is a collection of layers displayed in a cartographic projection and with basemap tiles for orientation – e.g. openstreetmap. I've kind of used "map" and "plot" to mean the same thing above. For examples for "maps", see e.g. at the bottom of [the xdggs healpix tutorial](https://xdggs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/healpix.html), or any of the examples in the [lonboard gallery](https://developmentseed.org/lonboard/latest/examples/)

coming back to this, I went with `zoom_to` for the method that takes cell ids and computes parent / child cell ids (I'm not entirely happy with that name, yet, so I'd still be open to change that). Note that this an operation that solely works on the cell ids and doesn't touch the data at all, so we still need #141 for that.

H3 doesn't support querying the children, yet, because `h3ronpy` returns either a flattened list of child cell ids or a flattened list of tuples (more accurately, a arrow table) of cell ids to child cell ids (depending on the method used). We thus would need an extra processing step to compute a 2D array of `cells × children` (doubling the memory use).

(side note: I've been thinking about adding some generic dask support to Xarray's `CoordinateTransform` / `CoordinateTransformIndex` and also about adding some abstract integration of Xarray's coordinate transforms in xdggs, which could probably reused in this context at some point. It is neither a bug nor an intentional choice I think. The original variable is passed so we can propagate its metadata, and of course we cannot pass the new (indexed) variable to the index's `create_variable()` which should create and return that variable.

> I'd have to figure out how to use the right dask chunks in create_variables

You'd need to track chunk sizes within the index so `HealpixMocIndex.isel()` can return a new index with new chunk sizes to be used in `HealpixMocIndex.create_variables()` to create the dask array.

@benbovy, this appears to work properly now. The current behavior is:
- if we detect a full domain (`obj.sizes["cells"] == 12 * 4**level`), we use a special constructor and don't look at the values
- if the data of cell_ids is not a dask array, we use `RangeMOCIndex.from_cell_ids`
- else we create a `RangeMOCIndex` for each chunk, then reduce using `RangeMOCIndex.union`

Missing functionality (compared to `PandasIndex`) is `isel` with arrays and `sel`, because I couldn't figure out how to implement those on MOCs so far.

I'll look into adding a few more tests before this is ready for merging.

FYI with #151 this works very quickly:
```python
import xdggs
import xarray as xr
import dask.array as dsa

# to make sure we don't compute
from xarray.tests import raise_if_dask_computes

zoom = 15
path = f"https://nowake.nicam.jp/files/220m/data_healpix_{zoom}.zarr"

ds = xr.open_dataset(path, engine="zarr", chunks={}).assign_coords(
    cell_ids=lambda ds: ("cell", dsa.arange(ds.sizes["cell"], chunks=ds.chunks["cell"], dtype="uint64"))
)
grid_info_mapping = {"grid_name": "healpix", "level": zoom, "indexing_scheme": "nested"}

with raise_if_dask_computes():
    decoded = ds.dggs.decode(grid_info_mapping, index_kind="moc")
```

The index itself is not really useful right now, though, and the different methods (`cell_centers`, `cell_boundaries`, etc.) don't support `dask` yet. It should be pretty easy parallelize these in a central place though because they are very embarrassingly parallel.

Note that using the name `cell_ids` for both the coordinate and the dimension will cause `xarray` to create a default `pandas` index, which we need to avoid (I think this is where the original example ran out of memory, even though `.decode` would have failed for the exact same reason).

indeed, the discussion was mostly in #62, but also in #64 and #65. The conclusion was that in the context of a grid (and `xdggs`, at least, only deals with grids) the name `level` is unambiguous.

'coarsen to' of course implies that you know which level you're at otherwise it might be void.

BTW 'refinement level' is the correct term for a specific grid instance in a DGGS from the SWG perspective. A possible issue with shortening it to 'level' is that there are many 'levels' in EO terminology. E.g. changing the 'refinement level' is different from changing the 'processing level'.

I believe I remember a discussion on 'resolution' somewhere on Github, but the issue tends to be forgotten and the term is hard to kill now that's so widely (and wrongly) used.

Regarding changing the gridding of data (aka 're-sampling'), that is always critical and requires certain conditions to be done safely. E.g. is coarsening only allowed if the coarser zone is populated in a representative way by finer samples (ideally it is continuously sampled). If some samples are missing that is okay as long as the remainder is not biased (no longer representative). Refining is even more complex, leads to far here...

Generally, please keep in mind that in the near future we will have to consider uncertainty in all operations we do with values (in fact 'data' consists always of 'value' and 'uncertainty', although the latter is often neglected). The effect of re-sampling on uncertainty is actually more important than the one on the values, and even if the values change only slightly, the uncertainty always increases which each re-sampling. That's why it should be limited to a minimum and done only with utmost care.
